💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Garbage-First Garbage Collector (G1) is the default garbage collector on the JVM as of JDK 27, with JEP 523: Make G1 the Default Garbage Collector in All Environments, which made it the default in all environments.
  • Industry observers note that G1 was originally introduced in JDK 6u14 as an experimental feature, promoted to a standard feature in JDK 7u4, and designated the default garbage collector in JDK 9, taking over that role from ParallelGC.
  • At the time of its introduction, G1 was designed for server environments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Garbage-First Garbage Collector (G1) is the default garbage collector on the JVM as of JDK 27, with JEP 523: Make G1 the Default Garbage Collector in All Environments, which made it the default in all environments. It had been the default garbage collector in "server" environments since JDK 9, with JEP 248: Make G1 the Default Garbage Collector. G1 seeks to balance throughput and latency and is a good option for many workloads. In this article, we will cover a brief history of G1, its key design concepts, and how to use it.

Industry observers note that G1 was originally introduced in JDK 6u14 as an experimental feature, promoted to a standard feature in JDK 7u4, and designated the default garbage collector in JDK 9, taking over that role from ParallelGC. While G1 has taken over the role of default garbage collector from Parallel, it was originally introduced to replace the CMS (Concurrent-Mark-Sweep) Garbage Collector, which was deprecated in JDK 9 and removed in JDK 14.

At the time of its introduction, G1 was designed for server environments. Systems using G1 were expected to have multiple processors and large amounts of system memory (tens of GB) available. Continued development of G1 has reduced its system requirements, and now G1 can provide good performance even in resource constrained environments with only a single CPU and less than 2 GB of available system memory. This is why, as of JDK 27, it is the default garbage collector across all system configurations.

Recent findings suggest that in garbage collector design, the three primary design constraints are throughput, latency (pause time), and memory footprint. G1 seeks to maintain a balance between latency and throughput, rather than heavily optimizing for either. By comparison, ParallelGC primarily focuses on maximizing throughput, and ZGC focuses on minimizing latency. G1 also aims for more consistent pause times than the CMS collector it replaced.

Recent findings suggest that as of the writing of this article, 12 JEPs relating to G1 have been delivered since JDK 8, with more changes planned for the future. Continued development has steadily improved G1's throughput, latency, and memory footprint.

G1 is a generational, incremental, parallel, mostly concurrent, stop-the-world, and evacuating garbage collector. For an explanation of each of these terms, check the Garbage Collection Concepts and JVM Collectors article on dev.java. This section covers some of the key design characteristics of G1.

Recent findings suggest that as mentioned in the previous section, G1 was originally designed with large "server-like" environments in mind. G1 is capable of efficiently marshalling the resources of systems with dozens of cores and addressing heaps measured in tens of GB.

Figure 03-01: Simplified representation of the G1 heap layout.

G1 divides the heap into a set of regions (increments) of uniform size. Figure 03-01 is a simplified example of what the G1 heap space would look like. The size and number of regions, unless otherwise configured, are based on internal heuristics, with the overall heap size being the primary influence on both. These regions are then divided up into eden, survivor, old, and humongous regions.

Sources indicate that eden and survivor regions are both part of the "young" generation. On creation, an object is placed in an eden region. If that object survives a collection, it is evacuated (copied) into a survivor region. Unreachable objects are not deleted individually; rather, the region they are a part of is considered empty and is eligible for reuse by G1. Surviving objects, if they remain reachable, will be evacuated to a new survivor region on subsequent collections. If an object survives enough collections, based on internal heuristics unless otherwise configured, it will be evacuated to an old region, which is checked less frequently.

A humongous region is a contiguous space of one or more regions, reserved for a single "humongous" object. An object qualifies as "humongous" if it's larger than half the size of a single region. Humongous objects bypass the eden and survivor regions and are treated as equivalent to an old region by G1.

Figure 03-02: Simplified representation of the G1 garbage collection cycle.

The G1 garbage collection cycle (GC cycle) consists of both stop-the-world and concurrent behavior, both of which can run in parallel. Again, check Garbage Collection Concepts and JVM Collectors for definitions of these terms. Figure 03-02 is a simplified visualization of the G1 GC cycle and will help to contextualize this section.

According to recent reports, at a high level, the G1 GC cycle consists of two phases: Young-Only and Space-Reclamation. G1 will start in the Young-Only phase, which, as the name suggests, means only young regions are collected. In G1, when a collection happens, the application is paused while G1 evacuates objects to upcoming regions or performs other GC work.

Sources indicate that the concurrent behavior of G1 is primarily concerned with determining which objects in old regions are still active. The concurrent phase can be broken into three distinct parts and starts when old-generation occupancy reaches a threshold.

Concurrent Start is the first step in the concurrent phase and is a special pause. During this pause, normal evacuation of young regions still occurs, and G1 also initiates concurrent marking of old-generation regions to determine which objects are still reachable. It is also possible that G1 determines there is no need to follow through with marking, in which case a Concurrent Mark Undo pause occurs, and the Young-Only phase continues.

According to recent reports, remark is the second step in the concurrent phase. This is a special pause where no evacuation of young regions happens. Instead, during this pause, G1 finalizes concurrent marking and performs other work, such as reference processing, class unloading, and reclaiming empty regions. Between this phase and Cleanup, G1 will concurrently calculate information to be used during the Space-Reclamation phase.

Industry observers note that cleanup is the third and final step in the concurrent phase. This is also a special pause where no evacuation of young regions happens. During this pause, G1 determines if it should proceed to the Space-Reclamation phase. If a Space-Reclamation phase is determined to be necessary, the Young-Only phase will complete with a single Prepare Mixed young collection.

Industry observers note that the Space-Reclamation phase consists of multiple mixed collections: collections where young and old regions are evacuated. G1 uses an efficiency algorithm to determine which old regions to collect first. A major factor in this algorithm is the amount of garbage in each old region, as regions with more garbage are more likely to yield large amounts of space. This is what "Garbage-First" in the G1 name refers to: it will reclaim the regions with the most garbage first.

In a recent development, the Space-Reclamation phase ends when G1 determines that evacuating more old regions is no longer worth the effort. At this point, G1 shifts back to the Young-Only phase.

For more technical details on G1, check the Garbage-First Garbage Collector guide and the G1 Stack Walker video at the bottom of this page.

It has been revealed that G1 is explicitly enabled with the JVM argument -XX:+UseG1GC. If you are on JDK 27 or later, this argument is never necessary, as G1 was designated the default GC in all environments. From JDK 9 to JDK 26, G1 was chosen by the JVM if it detected two or more CPU cores and more than 1792 MB of available system memory; otherwise, SerialGC was used. If you are on JDK 8, you will need to explicitly set -XX:+UseG1GC to use G1, as ParallelGC is the default GC.

According to recent reports, generally speaking, users should avoid applying too much configuration to garbage collectors. Often, "less is more," and the engineers who develop and maintain garbage collectors, G1 included, have worked toward having internal heuristics provide the best performance in most use cases "out of the box." As of the writing of this article, an upcoming change to G1, Automatic Heap Sizing, would handle one of the most important remaining aspects of G1 configuration: configuring the heap size.

Industry observers note that when thinking about configuring a garbage collector, consider the three major constraints garbage collectors are designed around: throughput, latency, and memory footprint. G1 aims for a balance between latency and throughput. When a user provides custom configuration to G1, some tradeoff will be happening. A user increasing the heap size is trying to trade a larger memory footprint for reduced latency. A user setting a higher pause time goal for G1 will be trying to trade reduced latency for improved throughput. As a user considers configuring G1, there are no settings for simply "better" performance, but, at best, a tradeoff. Some configuration combinations simply lead to worse observed performance. Below are some key configuration parameters for G1.

For a deeper dive into configuring G1, check the guide maintained by the G1 engineering team.

  • You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers.
  • Recent findings suggest that would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Recent findings suggest that would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

Recent findings suggest that in the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart promptly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

According to recent reports, as if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

Industry observers note that nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

Stable and comfortable at easy paces.

According to recent reports, why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Saucony Endorphin Speed has been one of the most influential running shoes of recent years, setting the template for fast training sneakers that uses some of the materials and tech from top carbon plate racers.

With the line proving so successful, Saucony has been reluctant to change much about the shoe over the five generations to date, and even though the Endorphin Speed 6 is the biggest update yet thanks to a new midsole foam, it mostly retains the same ride feel as past models.

I’ve reviewed every model of the Endorphin Speed and I’ve always been a substantial fan. While that’s still true with the Speed 6, this category contains some of the best running shoes available, and there are some lighter, bouncier fast trainers I rate very highly, like the New Balance SC Rebel v1 and Dynafish Xiaonian.

Industry observers note that the Saucony Endorphin Speed 6 costs $180 in the U.S. and £180 in the U.K., which is a $5 price rise on the Endorphin Speed 5. It’s an expensive shoe, though not out of line with other plated trainers like the Hoka Mach X3 and Newly introduced Balance SC Rebel v1.

Right now the Saucony Endorphin Speed 5 is widely reduced, dropping to $104 on Amazon in the Black Friday sales, which is a factor to consider when weighing up buying the Speed.

The Endorphin Speed 6 is presently available in five colors in the women’s shoe, and four colors in the men’s, including the white and yellow design I tested.

There is a wide version of the shoe available, though I found that the standard one fit me well in my normal running shoe size, the same size I’ve used with all past models of the shoe.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Saucony has added 2mm of foam to the midsole of the Endorphin Speed 6, which has a stack height of 38mm at the heel and 30mm at the forefoot, maintaining the 8mm drop of past models.

It weighs in at 8.5oz, which is 0.5oz lighter than the Endorphin Speed 5 in my size, a welcome drop for a speed-focused shoe.

The Endorphin Speed 6 has a simple mesh upper that has a little bit of padding around the tongue and collar, but mostly focuses on being lightweight and breathable.

It’s my preferred kind of upper on any shoe, since it’s not oppressively padded on the tongue or overly stiff around the heel, and I found the fit comfortable and secure throughout all my runs.

The Endorphin Speed 6’s main changes are in the midsole, which is made from a upcoming foam called PWRRUN PBX, which is meant to be lighter and bouncier than the PWRRUN PB that has been used on all past models of the shoe.

There’s also the higher stack and a redesigned nylon plate in the midsole, which aims to create a smoother, faster ride, with the Speedroll rocker on the shoe also contributing to this.

The changes to the midsole are noticeable on the run, though not as dramatically as I expected when looking at the spec sheet for the Speed 6.

Rubber is used sparingly on the bottom of the Speed 6 to keep the weight down, but patches cover the forefoot and heel of the shoe, and in my experience Saucony’s pelletized midsole foams are durable even when the foam is exposed on the bottom of a shoe.

Grip hasn’t always been a positive feature on the Speed line, but the Speed 6 provided me with reliable traction in wet conditions on both the road and the track during my testing.

After the very pleasant surprise of the original Endorphin Speed, which I ran over 300 miles in, I’ve found that the line has delivered a reliably similar experience with all of the models since.

There have been updates to make it more stable and comfortable, but ultimately all five versions of the Speed to date have had a smooth, fast and versatile ride feel.

This is still true of the Endorphin Speed 6 for me, and while that’s mostly a positive in that it performed well across a variety of runs in my testing, some might have hoped for a bigger change to challenge rivals like the SC Rebel v1 and cheaper, lighter options like the Adidas Adizero Evo SL and Dynafish Xiaonian.

I used the shoe for a couple of easy runs, two progression runs moving from easy to tempo pace, and a threshold track workout running 4 x 8min reps, and it felt great throughout.

I used the shoe for a couple of easy runs, two progression runs moving from easy to tempo pace, and a threshold track workout running 4 x 8min reps, and it felt great throughout.

The rockered midsole pushes you smoothly through your footstrike, and while the midsole foam isn’t as soft and springy as some, it does give a good amount of energy return off the toes.

I also found the Speed 6 to be quite stable and comfortable for easy runs, which is not always the case with plated trainers like this. I could happily use it for pretty much any kind of run, though it’s not as fast as a true carbon plate racer, or as comfortable as a max-cushioned cruiser.

To compare it directly to the Endorphin Speed 5 I did a short run wearing both shoes, and while the Speed 6 is a little bouncier and more comfortable, especially under the forefoot, I still felt the two shoes had a similar ride feel.

The Speed 6 is still a bit firmer than most super-trainers, and not as comfortable as more cushioned shoes under the toes. Some will like this more direct ride feel, but I appreciate the extra softness and bounce of a shoe like the SC Rebel v1.

If you’re a long term fan of the Endorphin Speed line the Speed 6 will be a winner. It’s a mild improvement on the previous models with extra cushion and bounce, and delivers the versatile performance you expect from the line.

There is certainly a case for getting the Speed 5 instead in sales in my opinion, but the Speed 6 is a slightly better shoe overall and a successful enhancement.

The Speed line has been faced with increasingly fierce competition in recent years, and I don’t think the Speed 6 does much to change the equation on this front.

If you want a lighter, bouncier fast trainer, the Upcoming Balance SC Rebel v1 would be my pick, while plate-free shoes like the Adidas Evo SL, Dyanfish Xiaonian and the new 361° Mega 3 Pro all offer fast, fun rides at a lower price.

According to recent reports, as someone who would always have had the Endorphin Speed in my own rotation through the first few models, I’ve now moved on to shoes like this myself. Even though the Speed 6 is just as good as past models, I personally like the springier ride available in fast trainers.

Aqara has unveiled the global launch of six new smart lighting products with full Apple Home support and what the manufacturer describes as “spatial intelligence.”.

The newly introduced lineup includes a vertical floor lamp with 18 individually addressable lighting zones, and a new LED strip offering seamless color gradients, dynamic flowing effects, and music synchronization ….

All of the fresh products are Matter compatible, allowing them to fully integrate with Apple Home, in addition to supporting the full range of competing ecosystems: Amazon Alexa, Google Home, Samsung SmartThings, Home Assistant, and Homey.

With a compatible sensor like the FP400, all of the upcoming products support spatial intelligence.

This enables automation to respond not only to whether someone is present, but also to exactly where people are within a space and how they move through it. For example, the ambient lights can turn on and off based on your movement from the couch to the dining room table.

Its intelligent AI sensing algorithm drastically improves reliability by reducing false triggers caused by environmental factors like pets, airflow, and robotic vacuums. A built-in ambient light sensor also helps trigger smart home scenes based on both human activity and lighting conditions.

You might initially struggle to spot the latest products in the company’s new releases section on its Amazon store. That’s because instead of each having its own section, you need to click or tap on the product in the top image.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

Sources indicate that VWFNDR + MBL launched on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with.

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial enhancement.

In a recent development, on Android, this comes in the form of newly introduced color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

Colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

Here’s what the output looks like:.

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that chromebooks are distributed to students through a fence at a Los Angeles Unified School District high school for during the Covid quarantine.
  • Hundreds of workers at Google are pushing senior leadership to retract a policy that would block schools who turn off its Gemini AI tools from access to the organization’s search engine starting next year.
  • Sources indicate that google made the surprise announcement two weeks ago, on Election Day, with executives saying they wanted to address teachers and parents’ concerns around AI in the classroom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that chromebooks are distributed to students through a fence at a Los Angeles Unified School District high school for during the Covid quarantine. Sarah Reingewirtz/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News/Getty.

Hundreds of workers at Google are pushing senior leadership to retract a policy that would block schools who turn off its Gemini AI tools from access to the organization’s search engine starting next year.

Sources indicate that google made the surprise announcement two weeks ago, on Election Day, with executives saying they wanted to address teachers and parents’ concerns around AI in the classroom. Since then, communities across the country have protested Google’s tight hold on tech in many schools.

As I wrote last week after attending a rally in Fresh York City:.

It has been revealed that attendees of all ages held signs reading, “NO AI IN MY SCHOOL!”, “A.I. Gets an F,” “Stop stealing our imaginations,” and “SCHOOL Librarians = THE BEST Search Engines.” Some students handed out fliers to passersby while younger children ran around and drew pictures off to the side.

Many cars driving by honked their horns in support, and a few construction workers on the other side of the one-way street cheered the protesters on.

That day, protests took place in six other cities—Los Angeles; Chicago; Boston; Portland, Oregon; Boulder, Colorado; and Durham, North Carolina—all organized by a nationwide alliance of parent and community advocacy organizations.

According to recent reports, school districts across the country use the manufacturer’s software and Chromebooks, which were more affordable than Windows and Apple computers when many were quickly assembling remote learning programs during the early years of the Covid pandemic. The Chromebooks have built-in AI classroom tools, and Google Search embeds AI Overview and AI Mode powered by Gemini.

Responding to the backlash, three of the largest school districts in the US—New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago—are now discussing alternative search engines.

“Any opportunity to drive positive change with AI in education will rely on educators having the freedom to choose how to implement it in their curriculum,” employees wrote in a petition brought by the Alphabet Workers Union, which represents more than 1,000 workers at Google’s parent manufacturer. “Cutting off access to Search for schools that don’t wish to use AI will not help persuade our people, and will more likely result in them shutting out Google products altogether.”.

“It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products,” they continued, addressing Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Google vice president and general manager of education Chris Phillips, and Elizabeth Reid, its vice president and head of search.

Recent findings suggest that A software engineer in Google’s education department told me on Thursday that most workers did not know about the Google Search decision before it was publicly confirmed. Corporate leadership has now acknowledged the letter but has not responded to any of its specific demands.

AI classroom tools should be “built responsibly and prioritize the best interests of the students, not the firm’s bottom line,” the Google engineer stated.

Another engineer and union member in Fresh York, who also signed the petition, said to Mother Jones that the executive team “seems convinced that resistance to AI adoption is because people don’t see the vision.”.

That goes beyond teachers, parents, and students: the Google staffer remarked their colleagues are also concerned about how the tech giant is implementing their work on AI tools.

“If the tech is really as useful and desirable as they think it is, why don’t they trust us to choose to use it on our own terms?” the engineer asked.

Google has been contacted for comment.

Recent findings suggest that leaker Ice Universe says Apple is currently developing four models of the 20th anniversary iPhone which we’ve been referring to as the iPhone 20. We’re expecting next year’s flagship models to be a radical newly introduced design with an all-glass appearance.

Why four models rather than two is unclear, but it seems possible Apple is testing two versions of both the Pro and the Pro Max to determine just how ambitious it can be with the final product ….

Didn’t the iPhone 6 or the iPhone 11 already have a curved front glass?

According to recent reports, ice Universe states that two of the four models have quad-curved glass backs and two have flat glass. They indicate that Apple has already had to ramp back its ambitions with the curvature.

Apple is currently developing four models in total: two with flat glass backs and two with quad-curved glass backs. Apple has been prototyping this quad-curved design for three years, making several revisions along the way—particularly regarding the glass curvature, which is still being refined. The earliest version had a very pronounced curve; it was later reduced somewhat.

It’s standard practice for Apple to develop multiple competing prototypes of new devices, evaluating them for everything from usability and durability to ease of manufacturing.

We’re expecting Apple to use a combination of ultra-thin bezels and curved glass to create the illusion of no bezels at all – a more sophisticated version of the effect seen on the Apple Watch. Today’s report says the bezels are around 1mm thick.

According to recent reports, the curved edges on the quad-curved version are approximately 1mm wide. However, because the glass curves around all sides, when viewed straight on from the front, the bezel becomes nearly invisible, creating a near‑borderless appearance. #16555. Trump Got Played by Putin and Xi

Trump Got Played by Putin and Xi

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump promised a “historic trilateral meeting.” He failed to deliver.
  • The American president billed Thursday’s summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin as an opportunity to resolve intractable conflicts and bitter economic disputes through his signature brand of personal diplomacy.
  • But Trump’s need for public validation has always been a vulnerability, and America’s smartest opponents know how to exploit it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump promised a “historic trilateral meeting.” He failed to deliver.

The American president billed Thursday’s summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin as an opportunity to resolve intractable conflicts and bitter economic disputes through his signature brand of personal diplomacy.

But Trump’s need for public validation has always been a vulnerability, and America’s smartest opponents know how to exploit it. In China, Trump made a spectacle of himself fawning over authoritarian leaders who view the United States as a rival. They left with diplomatic legitimacy and strategic breathing space. He left with little to show in return.

“Peace through strength,” the White House posted on official social media channels, over a video of the three leaders meeting in Shenzhen, a major financial and technology hub in southern China.

Why viewers were meant to understand three old men in suits — Xi, Putin, and Trump are 73, 74, and 80 years old, respectively — walking down a hallway in slow motion as a projection of American strength is anybody’s guess.

“A meeting in search of an agenda,” The Guardian dubbed it.

“A meeting that could have been an e-mail,” a former British diplomat observed.

Critics and supporters alike speculated the gathering might become a “Upcoming Yalta,” invoking the 1945 summit where the “Massive Three” — Franklin Roosevelt, Joseph Stalin, and Winston Churchill — negotiated the shape of the postwar world. Those talks charted a course for a new international order, built around the United Nations, national sovereignty, and collective security — which despite immediately running aground on Stalin’s violated promises to permit free elections in Eastern Europe, had more or less survived to the present.

It has been revealed that there were fears that a modern “Big Three” would formally abandon that system altogether in Shenzhen, in favor of classic Great Power competition and spheres of interest. Each leader has their own interest in limiting the reach of international institutions. Instead, Shenzhen was a snoozefest: long on photo ops, short on substance. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

Yesterday’s crowning achievement was the “China-Russia-United States Heads of State Declaration toward Peace,” which having lived and worked in China, I can assure you sounds better in Mandarin. At least, you can say it faster —《中俄美三国元首和平宣言》or “Zhōng é měi sānguó yuánshǒu hépíng xuānyán” — which amounts to the same thing.

I’ve read it so you don’t have to. It notes the three countries should cooperate on UN reform, stable energy markets, limiting abuses of International Criminal Court (ICC) jurisdiction, and avoiding nuclear war.

Sharp-eyed readers will note that one of those items is curiously specific.

Given Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine and the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, there are surely more pressing concerns than the ICC’s jurisdiction.

The court has no independent police force, and relies on member states to execute warrants. It has never issued warrants for American or Chinese citizens, but it did so recently for Putin and a crop of his cronies. That complicates his ability to travel, if nothing else, so statements decrying the ICC and calling on states to disregard its jurisdiction are a de facto gift to the Russian president. Related Content Your Favorite THC Drinks Are About to Be Illegal Trump Says He Wants to Protect ‘My Friend’ Putin From International Courts Summer Walker Files $20 Million Cross-Complaint Against Interscope Julio Iglesias Under Investigation for Sexual Abuse Claims.

It’s also a boon to Trump, whose administration has made opposition to the ICC a rallying cry. The court is a convenient punching bag for skeptics of “globalism,” from Trump and his MAGA base to revisionist powers like China and Russia. What authoritarian leader doesn’t want their state officials shielded from international prosecution?

Certainly it was easier for the three leaders to launch an attack on international law than tackle the contentious problems that could have been on the table. Consider the trade war sparked by Trump’s tariffs on China, the wars in Ukraine and the Persian Gulf, or competition over artificial intelligence.

The race to control advanced semiconductors, computing capacity, and the most powerful AI systems are already a major source of tension between Washington and Beijing. Control of semiconductor production could well become the proximate cause of a shooting war, while AI-enabled weapons are already killing humans on the battlefield. Meanwhile, rogue or maliciously employed AI agents pose a threat somewhere between “the website is down” and “civilization-ending.”.

Sources indicate that how the competition over AI plays out could well shape economic and military power for generations, and for the moment, the United States appears to be leading the race. Yet the summit produced no public commitment on AI, and certainly nothing to ensure America retains its lead.

Sources indicate that that AI was discussed but didn’t make the final cut claims a lot about the dangers of the Trump presidency, even in its lame duck twilight years. Trump isn’t good at the painstaking work of diplomacy. Even if he is not experiencing a serious age- and/or dementia-related mental decline — and there are indications he may be — he has never been good at focusing on details, or sustained attention. Under Trump, the world is missing out on opportunities for peace and progress.

Xi and Putin are playing a much longer game. They understand that Trump has been humbled by his party’s defeat in the midterm elections, that he is constrained, and that his presidency has a finite horizon. Theirs is not. Neither leader has reason to engage with Trump on contentious matters as they wait to see what will come next in Washington.

It has been revealed that trump, as ever, mistakes personal chemistry for leverage. He embraced Putin and called him “my friend.” Xi received center stage presiding over the proceedings, later berating Trump in their one-on-one over Taiwan, warning Washington to “keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in U.S.-China relations.”.

In return, Trump received no commitments about issues that matter. No progress toward peace in Ukraine, no assurances about Taiwan, no help resolving the Iran war, no AI framework, no nuclear arms-control deal, no breakthroughs on tariffs or agricultural trade.

A former German diplomat observed ahead of the summit that the United States seemed to have forgotten one of its greatest strategic advantages: a global network of partners and allies, built over decades. Trump and his administration have worked tirelessly to alienate allies. In their place, he offers friendship to America’s rivals. Trending Stories Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake Some Gamers Are Pissed That ‘GTA VI’ Makes Them Be Nice to Their Girlfriend Trump Got Played by Putin and Xi.

In a recent development, the Shenzhen summit was historic, in the narrow sense that it had never happened before. Trump put the authoritarian leaders of China and Russia on a pedestal beside the American president. He legitimized Putin, gave Xi a grand stage, and presented both as equal partners in managing the world.

He made concessions in exchange for spectacle. And he forgot that there’s a difference between historic and consequential.

‘Songs in the Key of Life’ at 50: Stevie Wonder Brings a Miracle to Madison Square Garden

💡 Key Takeaways

  • For the length of his show, however, that lament wasn’t quite true, at least inside the arena.
  • It has been revealed that wonder’s stated aim, from the title on down, was to create a work that encompassed life, the universe, and everything.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that “The universe is in alignment,” Stevie Wonder stated, sitting at his keyboard at Madison Square Garden Thursday night, a beret emblazoned with a Yankees logo on his head. “But on this planet, we are not.”.

For the length of his show, however, that lament wasn’t quite true, at least inside the arena. On the first U.S. stop of a brief 50th-anniversary tour, Wonder and a vast, multi-generational, virtuosic crew of musicians — including many of his children — recreated the entirety of 1976’s Songs in the Key of Life, an album that was always a realm unto itself, and pulled the audience as one into it. As Wonder dug into the songs, his voice uncannily strong at age 76, it was impossible not to feel renewed awe in the face of the album’s emotional and musical scope, its density of ideas, its unrelenting brilliance. Wonder’s sunglasses in the first set had a bejeweled starfield in the lenses, as if, in place of conventional vision, he’d opened a portal into the cosmic beyond. That felt about right.

It has been revealed that wonder’s stated aim, from the title on down, was to create a work that encompassed life, the universe, and everything. There are songs both bleak and uplifting about being Black in America, being human on Earth, being a parent and a child, and, of course, being a 205-year-old guy on Saturn chilling among “rainbow moonbeams and orange snow.” Then there’s the proggier-than-prog jazz-fusion instrumental, “Contusion,” which he set his musicians loose upon at MSG, and another vocal-free track, the pastoral, transcendent, jazz-chord-laden “Easy Goin’ Evening (My Mama’s Call),” performed onstage with Wonder’s own chromatic harmonica joined by a second harmonica player, Frederic Yonet, and melodica played by musical director Greg Phillinganes.

According to recent reports, wonder snuck more chords into individual songs than some rock bands managed in their entire careers, and the performances were a reminder that even the album’s most famous songs have musical surprises embedded in them — the melody and sentiment of “Isn’t She Lovely” can obscure its complexity, with its funked-out synth-bass, aching harmonica, and those airtight, breakneck signature drum fills. “Sir Duke” was impossibly buoyant, propelled by some of the greatest horn riffs ever written and the strutting lines of Wonder’s longtime bass player Nathan Watts, who also played on the original recordings. Watts somehow dug even deeper on the next song, “I Wish,” as did drummer Stanley Randolph, achieving oneness with two percussionists, Senfaub Stoney and Aaron Draper. The album’s more distant corners shone as well: the acid-funk of “All Day Sucker,” the rhythmic explosions of “Black Man,” or “Ebony Eyes,” which featured a battle between talkbox guitar and saxophone. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

Even after five decades, the album’s resurrection had little to do with nostalgia; Wonder was so present in the music that he wiped away tears during the opener, “Love’s in Need of Love Today.” After that song, he shouted out the power of democracy, mentioning New York City’s “new mayor.” And on the always wrenching “Village Ghetto Land,” with its brutal juxtaposition of “Eleanor Rigby”-like strings (played on synth by Wonder on the album, and by an actual string section in concert) against visceral descriptions of the horrors of ghetto poverty, he added an interjection: “still in 2026!”.

Industry observers note that phillinganes, who went on to work with Michael Jackson and many others, played on the original album as an 18-year-old, and has been helping Wonder remake Songs in the Key of Life onstage since 2014. He brings the same scholarly intensity to the recreation that the late Brian Wilson’s band gave to Pet Sounds, and these performances deserve a live album and, in an ideal world, the Sphere’s more precise sound system — some of the lovingly crafted details are inevitably obscured in echoey arenas. Trending Stories Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake Some Gamers Are Pissed That ‘GTA VI’ Makes Them Be Nice to Their Girlfriend Trump Got Played by Putin and Xi.

In a recent development, in his latter-day live shows, Wonder has a fondness for covers, medleys, call-and-response bits, and loose jams, all of which are mostly held at bay by the album-recreation format. Early in the show, he did depart from the track listing long enough to run through welcome segments of “Overjoyed” and “Uptight (Everything Is Alright),” combined with quirkier bits: the chorus of “Born in the U.S.A.” (by one of his fellow “We Are the World” vocalists), and a fairly lengthy take on “Love Me Do.” (It later emerged that both Paul McCartney and Bruce Springsteen were in the house, in a luxury box alongside Spike Lee and Dave Chappelle.).

It has been revealed that in the post-album encore, with a curfew looming, Wonder managed to deliver segments of “My Cherie Amour,” “Do I Do,” and “Living for the City” before unleashing a more full-fledged version of “Superstition” that broke past the venue’s strict 11 p.m. stop time. “I love you so much,” Wonder told the crowd, multiple times, and it felt like more than stage banter. “Take care of each other.”.

Latest Update: There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage.
  • That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public.
  • According to recent reports, but to skeptics of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

According to recent reports, but to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

It has been revealed that love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering upcoming security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

According to recent reports, mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find latest security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be stated for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October patch. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's notable to understand that just about every firm that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Recent findings suggest that barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one organization, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

Atlas Sound, the solo project of Deerhunter singer Bradford Cox, has emerged from a decade-and-a-half hiatus with the surprise fresh album Thanatos, out now digitally.

Arriving 15 years after 2011’s Parallax, Thanatos marks the third and final chapter in an album trilogy that began with 2009’s Logos; Cox himself had been out of the spotlight for the better part of seven years, as Deerhunter also hadn’t released an LP since 2019’s Why Hasn’t Everything Already Disappeared?

However, after a long musical dormancy, Atlas Sound reemerged this year with a couple of demonstrates, followed by the Halloween release of a new song titled “Octoberland”; that track now serves as the opener on Thanatos.

Cate Le Bon, who produced Deerhunter’s Why Hasn’t Everything Already Disappeared?, praised Cox in a statement that accompanied Atlas Sound’s new album.

“Bradford Cox has always existed in extremes. Embracing and transcending the contradictions inherent in an artist reaching for all the corners. Impossible to capture or imitate,” Le Bon said. “Each vocal take is a performance. Each instrument played like it’s his last night on earth. That could always be true. Without this awareness of mortality; love, passion and creation lose substance.”.

In a recent development, cox performed and recorded the entire 10-song album by himself “on a Tascam DP-008 in his attic in Grant Park, Atlanta.” “The Tascam, a tool to distil the process down to the fundamentals of subtraction and addition. The former a by-product of the latter. Nothing deleted but instead painted over with new emotion or the same gesture repeated with the urgency of the moment,” Le Bon added.

Along with Thanatos, record label 4AD — which will release the LP on vinyl next year — shared an intimate look into the life of Cox: Trending Stories Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake Some Gamers Are Pissed That ‘GTA VI’ Makes Them Be Nice to Their Girlfriend Trump Got Played by Putin and Xi.

It has been revealed that atlas Sound will return to more steady touring in 2027, including three festival gigs that Cox has already booked: Salt Lake City’s Kilby Block Party, Knoxville’s Significant Ears, and Barcelona’s Primavera. However, things remain all quiet on the Deerhunter front.

iOS 27.3 debuts next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s newly introduced for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo users one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient newly introduced option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:.

Industry observers note that use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to promptly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

According to recent reports, if your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most customers, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

On a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo.

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

According to recent reports, you can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great fresh option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use.

Industry observers note that what should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that users have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a new setting so owners can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

By default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

According to recent reports, it’s not exactly a “latest feature,” but iPhone Duo people will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and fresh keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:.

#16542. Tech Report: Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3328 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

It has been revealed that A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

In a recent development, “It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn rapidly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Sources indicate that miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

Industry observers note that during totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Sources indicate that druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

Recent findings suggest that he photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

According to recent reports, he insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

According to recent reports, on the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

In a recent development, the corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very rapidly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, rolled out in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

According to recent reports, when Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

According to recent reports, it took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

Sources indicate that the error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” states Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller states wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

Sources indicate that if you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

Industry observers note that on the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller indicates with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” indicates Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

It has been revealed that as the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Industry observers note that twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Industry observers note that those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

According to recent reports, around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

Sources indicate that “That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” states Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

It has been revealed that for example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

In a recent development, with just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

According to recent reports, druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as swiftly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller indicates. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

Recent findings suggest that but for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller claims.

It has been revealed that who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.
